chunks: Buck IC: integrated vs external parts. The question: What components are typically integrated in the IC and which are typically external?
A buck converter IC puts the brains and, usually, the two power switches on one chip. The parts that store real energy or need accurate values stay outside.
That means the inductor, the capacitors, and usually two resistors that set the output voltage.
Bigger currents push you toward external switches, because the chip itself would get too hot.
Think of a small water pump station. The control box and the valves fit in one compact unit.
The big storage tank and the pipes are too large to hide inside, so they sit outside and you connect them. A buck IC works the same way.
The analogy has one gap: some chips also hide a few of the outside jobs, such as the parts that keep the control loop stable, while others leave them to you.
The IC (box) holds everything that decides when to switch and the switches themselves; the loop is closed through external passives.
The divider feeds back into the error amplifier, so its tolerance becomes your output accuracy.
Inductor: a coil that stores energy in a magnetic field and smooths the current. Power FET: a transistor used as a fast on/off switch for the main current.
Feedback divider: two resistors that scale the output down so the chip can compare it to its reference.
Bootstrap capacitor: a small capacitor that lets the chip turn on the upper switch, the one connected to the input.
Controller IC: a chip with the control logic but without the power switches.
Say you want 1. 6 volts out. The chip has a 0.
8 volts internal reference (a fixed, accurate voltage it compares against), and you use R 1 equals R 2 equals 10 kilohms in the feedback divider.
The chip adjusts the switching until the divider output equals 0. 8 volts, so the output is 0. 8 times (1 plus 1) equals 1. 6 volts.
You add an inductor, an input capacitor, an output capacitor and a small bootstrap capacitor. Everything else is already inside. That is the whole idea.
"The control brain is inside the IC: reference, error amp, oscillator, PWM comparator, protection, soft start and gate drivers.
For small and medium currents the two power FETs are inside too.
What stays external is energy storage and anything that needs tolerance: the inductor, input and output capacitors, the bootstrap cap, and the feedback divider on adjustable parts.
Compensation is internal on easy-to-use parts and external on flexible ones. For high current I'd switch to a controller with external FETs."
